The bundled demos

What Cards each bundled demo connects, how, and what happens when it runs. Choose "Open a Copy" from "Browse Demos" on the home screen and an editable copy is made in ~/Documents/Tsugumi/<demo> (the bundled original is not changed). The demos come as a Japanese set and an English set (demos/ja, demos/en), the same demos with their text in one language; the app shows the set of its language. The values below are from the English set, and the Japanese set gives the same numbers. Operations on screen are in Usage; kinds of Card and the rules of execution are in Features.

DemoSubjectWhat it shows
Data to reportAggregating a sales table into a reportReproduction by seed, failure and blocked, rerunning one Card with saved inputs, artifacts, child Workflows
Collatz (C++ / Python / Julia / R)The Collatz sequenceCross-checking independent implementations in four languages, branches, merges and loops, maxRuns, detecting integer overflow
Live StreamPlotting a random walk as it goesA stream made by a feedback loop, stopping at once, Dawn line charts
PlotsDiffusion of random walksOrdinary matplotlib (plt.show(), FuncAnimation) drawn straight into a Card; Plotly and Altair become interactive charts
Cas A · Chandra RGBX-ray observation of a supernova remnantObservation data pinned with Nix, rerunning per Card, version history
Science demosGravitational waves, a protein, an exoplanet, earthquakesFetching public data (sizes and SHA-256), analysing and plotting it
MNIST · comparing classifiersClassifying handwritten digits (seven methods, from kNN to a CNN)Seven branches from one input running at once in separate Nix environments and merging; rerunning just one branch with other conditions
Newton's methodNewton's method on the complex planeThe starting point decides where it goes and how fast; multiple roots and periodic orbits lose quadratic convergence
PharmacokineticsBlood concentration of a made-up drugThe dosing interval changes accumulation, peaks and troughs; the numerical solution is checked against closed forms (teaching material, not dosing guidance)
Maximum flow and minimum cutMaximum flow and minimum cutChecking max flow = min cut three ways, and that only bottlenecks change the flow
Dose–response curveA dose–response curve (synthetic data)Fitting a four-parameter logistic, with bootstrap intervals; the interval opens up when the concentration range does not bracket the EC50
Molecular propertiesProperties of published molecules (RDKit)Properties, structures and similarity from SMILES; paste a molecule to try it, and an invalid SMILES says why
Counting cells in imagesCounting cells (synthetic data and a real image)Scoring thresholding and watershed on images with known answers, and seeing where they break down
Survival analysisSurvival in lung cancer (lung from the survival package)How the hazard ratio moves with the subjects and the adjustment, side by side; checking the proportional hazards assumption
Meta-analysis: the BCG vaccineA meta-analysis of the BCG vaccine (dat.bcg from metafor)Fixed and random effects, heterogeneity, leaving one trial out, meta-regression on latitude
RNA-seq: airway and dexamethasoneRNA-seq (airway and dexamethasone)DESeq2 and edgeR compared on separate branches; whether to include the cell line changes the number of genes a lot
A correlation that reverses when stratifiedSimpson's paradox (penguins, and admissions at Berkeley)Correlations that reverse direction between the aggregate and the strata, and that which to read depends on the question
Scheduling a batteryCharging and discharging a battery (synthetic prices)How the optimal plan from dynamic programming changes with capacity and prices; at a flat price, not using it is optimal
Fluctuations in chemical reactionsGillespie's stochastic simulationHow it differs from rate equations; stationary distributions checked against theory; fluctuations growing as molecule numbers shrink
An inverse problem in heat conductionRecovering an initial temperature from measurementsThe naive inverse breaks down; how the strength of Tikhonov regularisation and the measurement time change the recovery
Comparing ecological modelsFur records of hares and lynx (1900–1920)Fitting predator–prey models and comparing them by AICc and by forecasting unseen years; a good score does not mean the mechanism is right
Draft versionsOnly the plans of the science demos above and of Cas AThe Agent generates Cards from Drafts, runs them and checks
Dynamical systems gallerySix dynamical systemsThe Agent splits independent Drafts among helpers and implements them at the same time
MNIST · comparing classifiers (Draft)Classifying handwritten digits (seven methods)From a plan implemented up to the data, helpers implement seven classifiers at the same time and the Agent puts the comparison together

The arrows in the diagrams are a Card's wires (output port → input port). The kinds of Card are trigger (where a run starts), input (an input whose value is edited on the Canvas), fork (distribution), branch (conditional branching), merge, subgraph (Card in Card) and code Cards (C++ / Python / bash / R / Julia). A fork Card only hands values out as the arrows show, so it is left out of each demo's table. Every Card has a summary in _meta.json, readable on the Canvas (by hovering, for trigger, fork, merge and branch) and in the Card's settings.

The basics

Data to report (report)

Makes a sales table from a seed, aggregates it by region into a Markdown report, and finally files it away in a child Workflow. The shortest Workflow, mostly Python Cards.

start → settings ─ share ─┬→ generate ─csv→ aggregate ─summary→ render ─report→ archive (child Workflow)
                          └──────────────── config ──────────────→ render
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends seed (42), rows (500) and heading
generatePythonWrites a CSV of rows rows of region, product, quantity and unit price with random numbers from seed. The same seed gives the same CSV
aggregatePythonTotals sales and quantity per region. With fail_on_purpose On, it fails on purpose (recordIO records its input and output values)
renderPythonWrites report.md and summary.json into a directory and displays the report (retainArtifact keeps the artifact)
archivesubgraphThe bash Card inside, copy, duplicates the report's directory and adds ARCHIVED_AT

Try

  • Change seed or heading and run. With the same seed the aggregate is the same and only the heading changes.
  • Turn fail_on_purpose of aggregate On and run. aggregate's log gives the reason, and render downstream is blocked. Turn it Off and rerun only aggregate: with the saved inputs it succeeds at once.
  • Double-click archive to go into the child Workflow, and preview and export the artifact's directory. Artifacts remain even after the run cache is cleared.

Collatz (C++ / Python / Julia / R) (collatz)

The same Collatz iteration implemented separately in C++, Python, Julia and R, checking that the four sequences agree. The iteration itself is drawn with the Cards' wires, so the behaviour of branches, merges and loops can be followed on the Canvas.

                        ┌→ collatz-cpp (child Workflow) ─┐
start → initial ─ both ─┼→ collatz-py  (child Workflow) ─┼→ compare ─sequence→ record
                        ├→ collatz-jl  (child Workflow) ─┤
                        └→ collatz-r   (child Workflow) ─┘

The outer Cards:

CardKindWhat it does
initialinputSends the starting value (27)
collatz-cpp / collatz-py / collatz-jl / collatz-rsubgraphIterates in the Workflow inside and returns the sequence until it reaches 1
comparePythonChecks that the four sequences agree exactly and passes the sequence on
recordPythonWrites the sequence to collatz.csv (k, a_k, parity) and keeps it as an artifact

Inside the child Workflow (the same shape in all four):

(boundary input n) → loop ─ split ─┬→ check ─value / even→ route ─a (even)→ halve ─┐
                      ↑             └→ collect → (boundary output sequence) └b (odd)→ triple ─┤
                      └──────────────────────────── half / triple ──────────────────────────┘
CardKindWhat it does
loopmergeMerges the first value with the values coming back from halve and triple
checkcodeOutputs nothing if the value is 1 (ending the loop); otherwise outputs the value and its parity. maxRuns (200) bounds the iterations
routebranchFires only a (halve) for even, or only b (triple) for odd
halve / triplecodeCompute n/2 and 3n+1. triple fails with integer overflow beyond 64-bit integers
collectcodeCollects and displays the values that arrive, and outputs the sequence when 1 arrives. C++ and Python clear the resident worker's state for each run in onRunStart

How the Julia and R sides differ. Julia and R Cards run in a separate process per invocation and remember nothing (Limitations). So collect cannot collect values; instead the value going back to loop carries "the sequence so far" (Walk: value and path), and collect outputs path as the sequence when 1 arrives. Because the message carries the process, the record of any Card shows the sequence up to that point.

R's range. R's numbers are doubles, so integers are exact only below 2^53. Larger values are passed by the worker as strings, so R's check and halve fail rather than round silently, and triple fails before computing when 3n+1 would reach 2^53. Within this range the four sequences agree. Julia computes in 64-bit integers (UInt64), and its triple, like C++ and Python, fails with integer overflow when 3n+1 exceeds 64 bits.

Try

  • Run it as it is. 27 reaches 1 in 111 steps (112 values), with a maximum of 9232 on the way. compare reports that they agree.
  • Set initial to 2: the odd side's triple is never chosen and is skipped.
  • Make maxRuns of check inside smaller: it stops at the iteration limit (execution_limit). With a starting value for which 3n+1 exceeds 64 bits, integer overflow is detected.
  • Set initial to a large value such as 2^60: R's check fails, saying it is "not below 2^53" (Julia, C++ and Python return 61 values).
  • Open collatz-jl or collatz-r and look at the record of collect: each invocation's display is the sequence so far.

Live Stream (live-stream)

Makes one value of a random walk every 100 ms and draws the latest values as a line chart in real time. A feedback loop that sends "the next state" back to itself makes a stream that ends.

start → settings ─state→ loop → generate ─sample→ plot
                          ↑         │
                          └─ next ──┘
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends seed (7), samples (200), interval_ms (100) and the initial state
loopmergeMerges the initial state with the next state generate returns
generateC++Waits interval_ms, then takes one step with a random number decided by seed and the index, and outputs the value and the next state. After samples it stops outputting the next state and the stream ends. It checks for stopping while waiting too
plotPythonDraws the latest window (60) values and their mean with a Dawn (WebGPU / Metal) line chart

Try

  • Run it and stop (Cancel) in the middle. It stops at once, and the chart up to that point stays.
  • Change interval_ms, seed, samples or window of plot and run again. The series resets, and with parallelism 1 or 2 no value goes missing or out of order.

Plots (plots)

Makes random walks and plots them with the same matplotlib, Plotly and Altair code you would write anywhere else. No Tsugumi-specific drawing calls are used. Python Cards use the SDK's matplotlib backend, so a figure drawn with plt.show() appears as the Card's display. Plotly's fig.show() and Altair's chart.show() appear as interactive charts.

start → settings ─walk→ simulate ─walks→ share ─┬→ summary
                                                ├→ diffusion
                                                ├→ explore
                                                └→ spread
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends seed (7), walkers (400) and steps (200)
simulatePythonMakes walkers ±1 random walks of steps steps with numpy
summaryPythonWith plt.show(), draws 40 trajectories with the ±2√t band, and a histogram of final positions with the normal distribution, in one figure
diffusionPythonWith FuncAnimation, plays live how the distribution at each time spreads as √t (frames frames)
explorePythonWith Plotly's fig.show(), a scatter plot of each walker's final position and farthest distance (coloured by the fraction of time above 0)
spreadPythonWith Altair's chart.show(), draws the mean squared distance growing in proportion to t, next to the theoretical value

Try

  • Run it: diffusion's display plays as an animation, and the last frame stays.
  • Enlarge the displays of explore and spread, and try zooming, hovering (values per walker) and the legend.
  • Change walkers, steps, seed or frames and run again.

Cas A · Chandra RGB (casa)

Pins with Nix the X-ray event data of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Chandra) and the analysis tool CIAO, and splits the photons into three energy bands for an RGB image. It also draws the energy spectrum of the same photons, to check which element's lines became which colour.

start → begin ─┬→ ciao ─tool──┐
               └→ load ─events┴→ bands ─images→ share ─┬→ rgb
                                                       └→ spectrum
CardKindWhat it does
ciaobashIn default.nix, builds the CIAO 4.18 source pinned by hash and passes on the store path and version. The build happens only the first time and takes a few minutes. The expression is read from gen740/ciao, pinned by commit and hash (nixSources of tsugumi.json; external Nix sources)
loadbashIn default.nix, fetches and unpacks HEASARC's observation file pinned by hash (explicit FTPS). The download happens only the first time; after that the file in the Nix store is used. It uses no network while running
bandsPythonSplits the photons into three bands, 600–1650 / 1650–2250 / 2250–7500 eV, and counts them with CIAO's dmcopy on a 360×360 grid centred on Cas A (RA 350.8584°, Dec +58.8113°). The total counted is checked against the number read with astropy, without CIAO. Writes a FITS file per band and provenance.json, and shows the photon counts as a table
rgbPythonAssigns the three bands to R, G and B and makes a PNG stretched with asinh (percentile 99.5, q 10). Records the display conditions and the PNG's SHA-256
spectrumPythonDraws a histogram of the energies of the photons in the same grid with matplotlib. Shades the three bands and marks the lines of Mg, Si, S, Ar, Ca and Fe

Try

  • Run it as it is. The default observation is ObsID 25628 (2.1 ks, 13 MB). bands shows the photon counts per band (red 101,187 / green 157,471 / blue 110,852) as a table.
  • Change obsid, file and hash of load to ObsID 114 (2000, 50 ks, 520 MB) or ObsID 19606 (2019, 49 ks, 349 MB): the deeper observations give a sharper image, and about twenty years of change can be compared (the values are on the sticky note and in load's description). Only the first run takes time to fetch.
  • Change the bands of bands, the stretch of rgb, or the range and binning of spectrum, and rerun just that Card. The spectrum shows that the green band contains exactly the Si line, and everything from S up falls in blue.
  • Open the version tree. It holds the process of trying bands, grids and stretches: failed branches, branches not adopted, the adopted version rgb-v1, the version that added the spectrum on top, and the version that pinned CIAO (Versions).

Science demos (fetching and analysing public data)

Four demos with the same shape: load fetches data from its publisher, and the two Cards that follow analyse it into figures and tables.

start → load ─data→ (analysis 1) → (analysis 2)

load is a Python Card allowed the network (network: true). It fetches the files of urls and names, passes them on as a folder, and shows the size and SHA-256 of each. Where Cas A's load pins the fetch with Nix, these fetch on every run.

DemoData fetchedAnalysis 1Analysis 2
GW150914 · gravitational waves (gw150914)GWOSC's H1 and L1 strain data (4 kHz, 32 s of HDF5)whiten: whitens with the PSD of a 4 s Welch estimate, applies a band-pass from f_low to f_high (35–350 Hz), and plots the waveform around the eventchirp: shifts L1 by ±10 ms to find the delay that best overlaps H1, overlays them, and shows the chirp in H1's spectrogram. Also estimates a rough SNR
6LU7 · a protein and its binding pocket (protein-6lu7)6LU7 from RCSB PDB (the SARS-CoV-2 main protease with the inhibitor N3)structure: takes out the coordinates of the Cα atoms and the inhibitor (chain C) and shows them as a 3D point cloud (Cα blue, inhibitor red)pocket: tables the residues within cutoff (4 Å) of the inhibitor and marks the pocket's residues on a contact map. You can check that the catalytic His41 and Cys145 are among them
Kepler-6 b · an exoplanet transit (exoplanet-transit)MAST's quarter-3 light curve of Kepler-6 (KIC 10874614) (FITS)detrend: normalises the points with quality flag 0, removes the trend with a moving median of window_days days, and searches for the period with Box Least Squaresfold: folds the phase by the period and finds the planet-to-star radius ratio Rp/R* = √δ from the depth δ of the dip (a period of about 3.23 days, a depth of about 1%)
Japan Trench · hypocentre sections and the b-value (seismic-trench)USGS hypocentres of M4 and above, 2000–2024, 34–42°N and 138–146°E (CSV)section: cuts out the band of latitude from lat_min to lat_max and draws a map of epicentres and a longitude–depth section in which the subducting Pacific plate showsb_value: plots the cumulative frequency log10 N(≥M) and finds the b-value of the Gutenberg–Richter law by maximum likelihood (Aki–Utsu) above mc

Try: run it as it is, then change a parameter of an analysis Card (the pass band, cutoff, window_days, the band of latitude, mc and so on) and rerun just that Card. The analysis alone is redone with the saved inputs, without fetching again.

Demos that compute locally

Demos that use no network while running. Their data is synthesised, comes bundled with a package, or is pinned with Nix (fetched once, at build time). Their runs are checked by tests with TSUGUMI_TEST_DEMO_RUNS=1.

MNIST · comparing classifiers (mnist-classifiers)

start → load → prepare → share ─┬→ knn ──────┐
                                ├→ logistic ─┤
                                ├→ svm ──────┤
                                ├→ forest ───┤
                                ├→ boosting ─┼→ compare → views ─┬→ tradeoff
                                ├→ mlp ──────┤                   ├→ recall
                                ├→ cnn ──────┤                   └→ hard
                                └────────────┘ (test images and labels)
CardKindWhat it does
loadPython (numpy, matplotlib)Pins the four MNIST IDX files with fetchurl and hashes in default.nix. Checks the headers and counts, and shows samples of each digit with the source. Uses no network while running
preparePython (numpy)Draws a stratified sample by seed, train_size (default 10000) and test_size (default 2000), scales pixels to 0–1 and passes them as an npz (a File port, kept as an artifact). Shows the count per digit
knnscikit-learnk-nearest neighbours (k). Shows the digits it got wrong and their neighbours
logisticscikit-learnLogistic regression (c, max_iter). Shows each digit's weights as an image
svmscikit-learnAn SVM with an RBF kernel (c, gamma). Shows the number of support vectors per digit
forestscikit-learnA random forest (trees, max_depth, seed). Shows an image of the pixels that mattered
boostingxgboostGradient boosting (rounds, max_depth, eta, seed). Shows the test error rate per round
mlptorch (CPU)A fully connected network with two hidden layers (hidden, epochs, seed). Shows how the loss went
cnntorch (CPU)A small network with two convolutional layers (channels, epochs, seed). Shows what the first layer picks out of test images
comparePython (numpy)Waits for all branches. Checks that they used the same test images (digest), recomputes the accuracy from the predictions to cross-check, and shows a ranking and, in words, whether the gap between first and second means anything
tradeoffPlotlyA scatter plot of accuracy against training and prediction time (log axes, Pareto-optimal points joined by a line, details on hover)
recallmatplotlibA table of recall by model × digit
hardmatplotlibThe 32 test images that the most models got wrong, and the most common wrong answers

Each classifier Card shows its accuracy, single-thread CPU time (training and prediction) and a breakdown of its mistakes, and passes its predictions for all test images to compare as a typed message (Result).

Try

  • Run it as it is. The seven branches run at the same time (how many at once is "Parallel runs" in the settings, default 4). The accuracy on 2000 test images is svm 0.9705, cnn 0.9680, mlp 0.9625, knn 0.9500, forest 0.9475, boosting 0.9455 and logistic 0.9210, and compare says the gap between svm and cnn does not reach twice the noise.
  • Set max_depth of forest to 3 and run just that Card. No other branch runs, and only forest's accuracy drops, from 0.9475 to 0.7570.
  • To compare again, run from forest onwards ("Run from Here Downstream"). Only forest and what follows compare run, and compare compares the new forest result with the saved inputs of the other branches and share. The branches you did not change do not run, so their accuracy is the same.
  • Change k of knn, gamma of svm or epochs of cnn.
  • Increase train_size of prepare and see which classifiers benefit from more images and whose time grows (svm's and knn's prediction times grow).

The data is MNIST by LeCun, Cortes and Burges, fetched from PyTorch's mirror https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/.

Newton's method (newton)

Solves $z^3 - 1 = 0$ on the complex plane to see how the starting point decides where it goes and how fast it converges. Alongside estimates of quadratic convergence and a map of where each point converges, it shows cases that lose quadratic convergence and cases that do not converge.

start → settings → roots ─ share ─┬→ orbits ─errors→ order
                                  ├→ basins
                                  └→ trouble
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends the polynomial's real coefficients coeffs (highest degree first; default [1, 0, 0, -1]), the damping factor damping, tolerance and max_iter
rootsPythonFinds the roots, their multiplicities and the critical points without Newton's method, from the eigenvalues of the companion matrix (numpy.roots). Checks them by the relations between roots and coefficients, and for the form $z^n = c$ against the closed form too
orbitsPythonPlots the error against the iteration on a log axis, for each starting point start_re, start_im
orderPythonEstimates the order of convergence $q$ and its constant from the sequence of errors, and tables them next to the theoretical values set by the multiplicity and $\lambda$
basinsPythonStarts from every point of a grid and draws which root it reaches and in how many iterations. Zoom in with center_re, center_im and half_width
troublePythonShows side by side the reference case, near a critical point (offset), a multiple root, a multiple root brought back to quadratic with $\lambda = 2$, and a cycle of period 2 (the polynomials are fixed)

Try

  • Run it as it is. The errors in orbits fall quadratically on the log axis, and the estimated order in order lines up with the theory. basins draws the fractal boundaries between where points converge.
  • Set center_re of basins to -0.8 and half_width to 0.2 and rerun just that Card. Wherever you zoom on the boundary, all three colours gather.
  • Set offset of trouble to 1e-5. The first step is thrown out to $1/(3 z_0^2)$, and far away it comes back only by 2/3 per step, so the iterations go from 37 to 60 (exactly the default max_iter; smaller still, max_iter must be increased).
  • Set damping of settings to 0.5 and run the whole. From every starting point the order becomes 1 with ratio 0.5, and the shape of the boundaries on the map changes too.
  • Set coeffs of settings to [1, 0, -3, 2] ($(z-1)^2(z+2)$). At the root of multiplicity 2 the order drops to 1 with ratio 0.5, and the error stops at about $10^{-8}$.
  • Set coeffs of settings to [1, 0, -2, 2] ($z^3 - 2z + 2$). A black region appears around 0 (starting points drawn into a cycle of period 2 that never converge).

Pharmacokinetics (pharmacokinetics)

Compares how concentration moves with the dosing interval, in a one-compartment oral model of a made-up drug, "Tsugumicin". This is a made-up model for teaching. Its values are not those of any real drug, and it is neither medical advice nor dosing guidance. The therapeutic range is invented too.

start → settings → simulate ─curves→ share ─┬→ check
                                            ├→ window
                                            └→ missed
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends the dosing plans to compare (doses_mg, intervals_h), half_life_h, ka_per_h, volume_l, bioavailability, the invented therapeutic range (low_mg_l, high_mg_l) and days
simulatePythonSolves the differential equation with solve_ivp, split at each dose, and plots the concentration over time for the plans side by side with Plotly
checkPythonTables the superposition of closed forms, the steady-state accumulation ratio $R$ and the mean concentration against the numerical solution. Fails if they differ much
windowPythonOverlays the concentration in the last dosing interval and compares peaks, troughs and the fraction of time inside the therapeutic range
missedPythonPlots, with closed forms, the concentration per plan when missed_count doses from missed_at_h on are missed

Try

  • Run it as it is and look at window. 400 mg every 24 hours and 200 mg every 12 hours give the same mean concentration (the table in check), and shortening the interval narrows the gap between peak and trough.
  • Set missed_count of missed to 2 and rerun just that Card. For the same daily dose, the longer the interval, the more the time below the range grows.
  • Set half_life_h of settings to 16 and run the whole. The accumulation ratio grows, and so does the time to reach steady state.
  • Shorten days of settings and "reaching steady state" in check shows that it does not get there.

Maximum flow and minimum cut (max-flow)

On a made-up layered network made from a seed, checks that the maximum flow equals the minimum cut. You can compare which edges increase the maximum flow when widened, and which do not.

start → settings → network → flow → cut ─ share ─┬→ verify
                                                 ├→ whatif
                                                 └→ sweep
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends seed (53), layers, width, edge_probability and max_capacity
networkPythonMakes a layered directed graph with capacities from the seed (made-up data)
flowPythonFinds the maximum flow with networkx and draws each edge's flow/capacity. Checks capacities and conservation
cutPythonFinds the minimum cut with networkx and draws the $s$ side, the $t$ side and the cut's edges. Fails unless max flow = min cut
verifyPythonChecks that scipy's maximum_flow and brute force over all cuts give the same value, and counts the minimum cuts
whatifPythonRaises the capacity of an edge on the cut and one off it by raise_by, and tables the maximum flow and the new cut. edge (for example a1->b1) chooses the edge
sweepPythonFor every edge, bars the increase in maximum flow when its capacity is raised by raise_by

Try

  • Run it as it is and look at sweep. Of the cut's three edges only two increase it; a2->b2 does not, because another minimum cut remains (verify counts two minimum cuts).
  • Set edge of whatif to s->a2 and raise_by to 1000. Even an edge running at full capacity does not increase the maximum flow if it is off the cut.
  • Set edge of whatif to b3->c3. Raising it by 10 increases the flow by only 8, because the next cut gets in the way; increasing raise_by further gains nothing beyond that.
  • Change seed of settings and run the whole. On another network, the values in verify still all agree.

Dose–response curve (dose-response)

Makes plates of made-up compounds A and B with random numbers (synthetic data), fits a four-parameter logistic (Hill curve), and puts confidence intervals on the EC50 and the Hill slope. The true values are known, so you can check on the spot whether they were recovered. These are not real drugs, and this is not medical advice.

start → generate ─plate→ share ┬→ fit ─fit─────────→ bootstrap ─intervals→ compare
                               ├──────── plate ────→ bootstrap
                               └→ range
CardKindWhat it does
generatePythonMakes responses with normal noise on the true curve, from random numbers by seed. concentrations concentrations, diluted by dilution from top_um, with replicates replicates each
fitPythonFinds bottom, top, log10 EC50 and the Hill slope with scipy's curve_fit, and plots the data and the curve
bootstrapPythonFinds 95% intervals for the EC50 and the Hill slope by residual bootstrap (n_boot times), and tables whether they contain the true values. If an interval leaves the measured range, it warns, with the reason
comparePythonShows the ratio of EC50s (relative potency) with its interval, and the difference of Hill slopes. If the interval contains 1, it says "no difference can be claimed"
rangePythonRemakes synthetic plates changing only the highest concentration, and plots the width of the EC50 interval against it

Try

  • Run it as it is. The 95% intervals of the EC50 and Hill slope contain the true values, and the relative potency (true value 15) comes out as 14.4 (11.6 – 18.6).
  • Set noise_sd of generate to 12 and run. The intervals widen (for B's EC50, from 1.2-fold to 1.7-fold).
  • Set top_um of generate to 1 and run. B's curve never levels off, the interval's width exceeds 1000-fold, bootstrap warns "the concentration range does not bracket the EC50", and compare says "no difference in potency can be claimed".
  • Reduce concentrations or replicates. Change n_boot of bootstrap and rerun just that Card.

Molecular properties (molecules)

From SMILES, which writes a molecule as a string, computes properties with RDKit and lays out structural formulas, Lipinski's Rule of Five, a map of molecular weight and logP, and how alike the structures are. Paste a SMILES into paste on the Canvas and that molecule joins every Card.

start → paste ─pasted→ properties ─molecules→ share ┬→ structures
                                                    ├→ lipinski ─checked→ chemspace
                                                    └→ similarity
CardKindWhat it does
pasteinputSends name and smiles of a molecule to try (dopamine by default; with smiles empty, only the list is used)
propertiesPythonReads molecules (a list of "name: SMILES") and the pasted molecule, and tables molecular weight, logP (Crippen), TPSA, HBD, HBA and rotatable bonds. A SMILES that cannot be read is skipped, with the reason
structuresPythonDraws the structural formulas in a grid, with names and molecular formulas
lipinskiPythonChecks molecular weight ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, NH+OH ≤ 5 and N+O ≤ 10, and passes a molecule with at most max_violations violations
chemspacePython (Plotly)A scatter plot of molecular weight and logP. Hover to see the name, molecular formula, TPSA and the rules violated
similarityPythonA heat map of the Tanimoto coefficients of Morgan fingerprints (radius radius)

Try

  • Run it as it is. A table of the properties of 15 molecules and their structural formulas appear. Only atorvastatin and cyclosporin A fail the Rule of Five, and the most alike are morphine and codeine (Tanimoto 0.76).
  • Paste another SMILES into smiles of paste and run.
  • Set smiles of paste to C1CC( or C(C)(C)(C)(C)C and run. It does not crash: the reason it cannot be read appears above properties' table, and the other molecules are computed.
  • Set max_violations of lipinski to 0 and rerun just that Card. Cholesterol fails.
  • Set radius of similarity to 0 and rerun just that Card. The distinctions become coarse, and the average similarity rises.

Counting cells in images (cell-count)

Makes synthetic fluorescence-like images whose centres are known, counts the cells with thresholding and watershed, and scores the counts. You see what separating touching cells gains, and from where counting fails. The lower row applies the same procedure to a real image of nuclei (with no ground truth, it is not scored).

start → begin ┬→ generate ─scene→ share ┬→ preprocess ─cleaned→ segment ─labels→ score
              │                         ├──────────────── scene ───────────────→ score
              │                         └→ sweep
              └→ mitosis ─image→ real
CardKindWhat it does
generatePythonPlaces cells cells with random numbers from seed (touching_pairs pairs touch). Adds uneven illumination unevenness and noise noise
preprocessPythonEstimates and subtracts the background with a greyscale opening, and applies a Gaussian blur
segmentPythonFinds the foreground with Otsu's threshold and numbers its regions (threshold only), then separates them with watershed seeded at maxima of the distance transform
scorePythonMatches centroids one to one with the true centres and gives the count error, precision, recall and F1. Overlays what was found, what was extra and what was missed, for both methods
sweepPythonRemakes images with other numbers of cells and noise levels, and tables the same procedure's F1
mitosisbashPasses a fluorescence image of the nuclei of cultured human cells, pinned by its Nix hash (Moffat et al., Cell 2006, CC0; from scikit-image's data set; fetched once at Nix build time, no network while running)
realPythonApplies the same procedure to the real image and shows the counts and outlines

Try

  • Run it as it is. Against a true count of 80, threshold only finds 60 (recall 0.75) and watershed 74 (recall 0.93). On the real image of nuclei, threshold only finds 271 and watershed 311 (with no ground truth, check the outlines by eye).
  • Set cells of generate to 320 and run. Threshold only's recall falls to 0.24, while watershed keeps 0.79.
  • Raise noise of generate. As the top left of sweep's table shows, the fewer the cells, the more the threshold falls into the noise and overcounts.
  • Change min_distance of segment and rerun just that Card. Larger values separate less.

Survival analysis (survival)

With lung, bundled with the survival package (real data from the NCCTG advanced lung cancer trial, 228 patients; Loprinzi et al., J Clin Oncol 1994), finds Kaplan–Meier curves, the log-rank test and a Cox model. How much the same hazard ratio moves with "who is included" and "what is adjusted for" is laid out in one figure on the Canvas. These are associations in old trial data; they show no cause and are not advice.

start → load ─lung→ share ─┬→ cohort ─cohort→ split ─┬→ km
                           │                         └→ cox ─fit→ zph
                           └→ specs
CardKindWhat it does
loadRAdds event and female columns to lung, writes it as CSV, and tables each variable's median, range and missing values
cohortRChooses subjects by age_min, age_max and ecog_max. Shows the numbers of people and deaths next to the whole
kmRKaplan–Meier curves split by group (sex / ecog / age), medians and the log-rank test. Keeps the curves' values in curves.csv
coxRFits a Cox model with the variables in covariates and tables hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals
zphRPlots the scaled Schoenfeld residuals of cox.zph and shows p-values per variable and overall
specsRFinds the hazard ratio of exposure for every combination of subsets × adjustments and lays them out like a forest plot

Try

  • Run it as it is. Median survival is 426 days for women and 270 for men, and the log-rank χ² is 10.33. specs lays out the hazard ratios of 24 combinations of subjects and adjustments.
  • Read the figure in specs. The hazard ratio for women is 0.59 for everyone, but 0.76 (with an interval crossing 1) under 65 adjusted up to ECOG, and 0.39 for ECOG 2 and above adjusted for four variables. In the latter, missing weight-loss values reduce 51 people to 46.
  • Set group of km to ecog and run. The log-rank χ² changes from 10.33 to 18.98.
  • Add ph.karno to covariates of cox and run from cox onwards. The overall p-value of zph falls from 0.216 to 0.016, and the proportional hazards assumption becomes doubtful (in a single-Card run zph's input is not updated, so run on from cox).
  • Set age_min of cohort to 65, run, and look at how km and cox change.

Meta-analysis: the BCG vaccine (meta-analysis)

With dat.bcg, bundled with metafor (13 trials of the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis; Colditz et al., JAMA 1994), compares fixed-effect and random-effects pooling, heterogeneity and a meta-regression on latitude. How much the conclusion moves with choices such as leaving one trial out or changing the estimator can be seen on the Canvas. This is an example of statistical method, not advice about vaccination.

start → trials ─trials→ share ─┬→ pool
                               ├→ funnel
                               ├→ moderator
                               └→ sensitivity
CardKindWhat it does
trialsRFinds each trial's log risk ratio and variance from the counts (escalc), as a table and a CSV
poolRPools with fixed effect and random effects (method), and shows a forest plot with both diamonds, and I², τ² and Q. Trial numbers written in exclude are left out
funnelRA funnel plot with the regression test and the result of trim and fill
moderatorRRuns a meta-regression on moderator (by default the absolute latitude) and shows the slope, the residual τ² and the proportion explained in a figure
sensitivityRLays out the pooled risk ratio when each trial is left out in turn (fixed effect and DL), and with other estimators of τ²

Try

  • In the forest plot of pool, compare the fixed-effect diamond, 0.65, with the random-effects diamond, 0.49. I² is 92.1%.
  • Set exclude of pool to [8] (TPT Madras, the largest trial) and run only pool. The fixed effect moves from 0.65 to 0.48.
  • Set method of pool to REML. τ² changes from 0.309 to 0.313, but the pooled risk ratio hardly moves.
  • In moderator, see latitude reduce τ² from 0.313 to 0.076. Set moderator to year to compare.

RNA-seq: airway and dexamethasone (rna-seq)

With Bioconductor's airway (real data from four airway smooth muscle cell lines treated with dexamethasone; Himes et al., PLoS One 2014, GEO GSE52778), finds differentially expressed genes with DESeq2 and edgeR. How much "the number of differentially expressed genes" changes with thresholds and design can be checked in each Card. This is a cell-culture experiment; it shows no effect of treatment and is not medical advice.

start → load ─airway→ filter ─counts→ share ─┬→ normalize ─normalized→ pca
                                             ├→ deseq ─results→ fan ─┬→ volcano
                                             │                       ├→ thresholds
                                             │                       ├→ top
                                             │                       ├→ compare ←─results─ edger
                                             │                       └→ design
                                             ├→ edger
                                             └→ design
CardKindWhat it does
loadRWrites airway's count matrix (63,677 genes × 8 samples) and gene names as CSV, and tables the samples
filterRRemoves genes whose total reads are below min_total, and shows the distribution and the cut-off in a figure
normalizeRFinds size factors by median of ratios and compares the distributions before and after normalisation. Passes the vst on for the PCA
pcaRRuns a principal component analysis on the top_genes most variable genes, coloured by treatment and cell line
deseqRChooses ~ cell + dex or ~ dex by paired, writes DESeq2's results as CSV and draws an MA plot
volcanoRCounts by the fdr and lfc thresholds and draws a volcano plot, naming the genes in known
thresholdsRTables the number of genes for each point of a grid of FDR and log2FC
topRTables the top top genes by FDR, with the ranks of the known responsive genes in known
edgerRTests the same counts with edgeR's quasi-likelihood F test
compareROverlays the log2FC of DESeq2 and edgeR, and counts the genes found by both and by only one
designRAlso runs DESeq2 with ~ dex, and lays its estimates and statistics next to those of ~ cell + dex

Try

  • Run it as it is (the first time, the Nix builds of DESeq2, edgeR and airway take a while). compare shows 3985 genes on which DESeq2 and edgeR agree.
  • Read the figure in design. Including the cell line term increases the genes with FDR < 0.05 from 2713 to 4030. The log2FC hardly changes; only the statistics grow.
  • Change lfc of volcano from 1 to 2, or change fdr, and run only volcano. The counts match those in thresholds' table.
  • Set min_total of filter to 100 and run from filter onwards.
  • In top, look at the ranks of FKBP5, DUSP1 and TSC22D3. Ranking genes by FDR and by the size of their fold change do not give the same order (FKBP5 is 16.5-fold at rank 143; DUSP1 is 7.7-fold at rank 3).

A correlation that reverses when stratified (simpson)

A relationship seen in the whole can reverse its sign when split into strata. This is checked on two real datasets: the bill length and depth of penguins (palmerpenguins, Gorman et al. 2014) and applications to Berkeley in 1973 (R's UCBAdmissions). A note says that which value to read is not decided by the data alone, but by the causal question.

start → branches ─┬→ penguins ─penguins→ share ─┬→ correlate ─points, correlations→ figure
                  │                             └→ survey
                  └→ admissions ─admissions→ applications
CardKindWhat it does
penguinsRWrites the 342 birds with both bill length and depth as CSV, and tables the counts by species and island
correlateRSplits by stratify (species / sex / island) and tables r, its confidence interval and the slope for the whole and each stratum
figureROverlays on the same points the regression line for the whole (dashed) and the lines for each stratum
surveyRLays out r for the three stratifications in one figure, showing where it reverses
admissionsRTables the admission rates and odds ratios per department and overall, and the Mantel–Haenszel common odds ratio
applicationsRPlots admission rates as points sized by the number of applicants, with the overall rate as a dashed line

Try

  • Run it as it is. The r of bill length and depth is −0.24 overall, but 0.39, 0.65 and 0.64 within species: the direction reverses.
  • Set stratify of correlate to sex and run from correlate onwards. r stays negative in every stratum and does not reverse.
  • Set stratify to island. It stays negative on Biscoe, and turns positive on Dream and Torgersen.
  • In admissions' table, see the overall odds ratio of 1.84 become 0.90 when adjusted for department. In applications' figure, see how applications were skewed.

Scheduling a battery (battery)

start → settings → market ─ share ─┬→ schedule
                                   ├→ capacities
                                   ├→ tariffs
                                   └→ check
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends the capacity capacity_kwh (10), the power limit power_kw (3), the round-trip efficiency round_trip_efficiency (0.9), the export ratio export_ratio (0.5), the step of stored energy soc_step_kwh (0.1), seed (7) and days (7)
marketJuliaFrom the seed, makes a house's consumption, solar generation and three tariffs (flat, time-of-use, market-linked) per hour. States in the data and figures that all of it is made up
scheduleJuliaFinds the charging and discharging with the lowest electricity bill by dynamic programming with the stored energy as the state. Shows the price, charging and discharging, and stored energy under the tariff tariff
capacitiesJuliaSolves for other capacities and shows the saving, the saving per additional kWh, and how operation differs by capacity
tariffsJuliaRuns the same battery under four contracts and compares the saving, the number of cycles and how the stored energy moves
checkJuliaCompares with exhaustive search over a short period and a small battery, checks that at a flat price with exports at the same price it does not run, and tables the difference with a finer step. Fails if anything is off

Try

  • Run it as it is. Over the made-up week, with exports at half price, it saves about 786 yen even at the flat tariff, about 1478 yen with time-of-use and about 1442 yen market-linked. check shows dynamic programming agreeing with exhaustive search.
  • Change tariff of schedule to flat, tou or spot and rerun just that Card.
  • Lower round_trip_efficiency of settings and run. With time-of-use prices, once the efficiency falls below cheap / expensive (18 / 42), the round trip no longer pays.
  • Set export_ratio of settings to 1 and exports earn the same as imports cost, so storing solar is pointless. At the flat tariff the saving is 0 yen with 0 cycles: the battery does not run.
  • Change capacities_kwh of capacities and see where it levels off.

Fluctuations in chemical reactions (gillespie)

start → settings ─ share ─┬→ trajectories
                          ├→ stationary ─┐
                          ├→ scaling ────┼→ check
                          └→ binding ────┘
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends the synthesis rate synthesis (2), the degradation rate degradation (0.1), the volume volume (1), the number of runs runs (2000) and seed (1)
trajectoriesJuliaComputes runs runs with Gillespie's method and overlays shown_runs trajectories, the mean of all runs and the solution of the rate equation
stationaryJuliaCompares the distribution of end points after enough time with the theoretical Poisson distribution. Passes on the mean, variance and Fano factor
scalingJuliaMeasures the coefficient of variation at other volumes and compares it with the theoretical 1/√N. Also shows the trajectories converted to concentrations, per volume
bindingJuliaComputes A + B ⇌ C at other volumes and compares the fraction bound with the exact solution (detailed balance) and the rate equation
checkJuliaCompares the three results with closed forms and tables how many standard errors off they are. Fails beyond limit_sigma

Try

  • Run it as it is. The trajectories fluctuate, but the mean of 2000 runs follows the rate equation. The stationary mean and variance are close to the theoretical 20 (20.15, 20.46), and the Fano factor is 1.015. With two of each, A + B ⇌ C has a fraction bound of 0.57, off from the rate equation's 0.50 (it approaches it as the volume grows).
  • Set volume of settings to 0.1 and run. It becomes a Poisson distribution with mean 2, and trajectories drop to 0 too. The Fano factor stays 1.
  • Increase shown_runs of trajectories and rerun just that Card.
  • Change on_rate or concentration of binding and see how far it departs from the rate equation.
  • Make limit_sigma of check smaller and see how far statistical fluctuation takes it off.

An inverse problem in heat conduction (heat-inverse)

start → settings → forward ─ share ─┬→ spectrum
                                    ├→ naive
                                    ├→ tikhonov ─choice─┐
                                    ├────────────────── reconstruct
                                    ├→ horizon
                                    └→ check
CardKindWhat it does
settingsinputSends the grid cells (100), the thermal diffusivity alpha (1), the measurement time final_time (0.002), the noise noise (0.2 °C) and seed (3)
forwardJuliaMakes a made-up initial temperature, computes the temperature at time T by eigendecomposition of the finite-difference matrix with insulated ends, and adds noise. Checks that the total heat is conserved
spectrumJuliaShows how the singular values decay at each time, and the index of the mode where the measurement's components sink into the noise
naiveJuliaShows that multiplying by the inverse matrix as it is diverges (even without noise, by rounding error)
tikhonovJuliaSweeps λ and shows the L-curve and the error. Compares the discrepancy principle, the corner of the L and the λ closest to the truth
reconstructJuliaLays the recovery with the chosen λ (the discrepancy principle's value when lambda is 0), and with too small and too large a λ, next to the truth
horizonJuliaRecovers from the same noise at other measurement times, showing that the later it is, the more detail is lost
checkJuliaTables checks of the conservation of total heat, the analytic solution of a cosine mode, agreement with an implicit scheme, recovery without noise at an early time, and the maximum principle. Fails if anything is off

Try

  • Run it as it is. The naive inverse diverges to as much as 3.8e+33 °C, while Tikhonov regularisation recovers the shape with an error of 5.1 °C. In horizon, the later the measurement, the fewer modes stay above the noise (from 37 to 3), and the error grows from 1.9 °C to 10.6 °C.
  • Set final_time of settings to 0.02 and run. With the same noise, the recovery's error grows.
  • Change lambda of reconstruct and rerun just that Card. Back at 0, it uses the discrepancy principle's value.
  • Set noise of settings to 0 and final_time to 0.00005, and the recovery returns to the truth.
  • Change times of horizon and find the time at which the jaggedness disappears.

Comparing ecological models (ecology-models)

start → load ─ share ─┬→ fit ─ fits-share ─┬→ check
                      │                    ├→ phase
                      │                    └→ scores
                      └→ forecast ────────────→ scores
CardKindWhat it does
loadJuliaReads the Hudson's Bay Company fur records (thousands of pelts, 1900–1920) from a CSV bundled with the Card, and shows them with the source
fitJuliaMinimises the squared error of logs with Nelder–Mead while solving three models with RK4 (in log space, from restarts starting points, up to the year fit_until). Finds AIC, AICc and BIC and overlays the fits on the records
forecastJuliaFits up to fit_until (1914) and compares the errors in forecasting the years held out
scoresJuliaTables log RMSE, AIC, AICc, BIC, forecast error, the number of starting points that reached the same solution, and the best values
phaseJuliaExtends each model's best solution years years ahead and compares them in a phase diagram
checkJuliaChecks RK4 against the Lotka–Volterra conserved quantity, and compares the fitted values with the posterior of the Stan case study

Try

  • Run it as it is. Over these 21 years the three models fit almost equally (log RMSE 0.219), AICc favours Lotka–Volterra with the fewest parameters, and Holling's handling time h goes towards 0. The error of forecasts fitted up to 1914 is also smaller for Lotka–Volterra (0.353, against 0.421 for the others). The sticky note says that a good AIC does not mean the mechanism is right, and that pelts are not population counts.
  • Change fit_until of forecast between 1908 and 1918 and rerun just that Card. The more years held out, the harder the forecast.
  • Lower or raise restarts of fit and look at "starting points that reached the same solution" and the errors in scores.
  • Increase years of phase and see where the logistic spiral heads.

Draft versions (for the Agent to implement)

casa-draft, gw150914-draft, protein-6lu7-draft, exoplanet-transit-draft and seismic-trench-draft are projects that hold the same plans as the demos above, as Drafts only (casa-draft is the plan up to the RGB image, without CIAO and spectrum). Each has a start Card and three Drafts, and each Draft's description says what it receives, what it does and what it passes on (almost the same text as the descriptions of the implemented demos' Cards).

Press "Generate Cards" at the top right of the Canvas and the Agent makes Cards from the Drafts, runs them and checks (Generating Cards from Drafts).

Dynamical systems gallery (dynamics-draft)

A demo in which the Agent splits six independent Drafts among helpers and implements them at the same time.

start → settings ─ share ─┬→ lorenz      the Lorenz attractor (RK4, density in the x–z plane)
                          ├→ mandelbrot  the Mandelbrot set (smooth colouring)
                          ├→ logistic    the bifurcation diagram of the logistic map
                          ├→ life        the Game of Life (200 generations on a torus)
                          ├→ grayscott   Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion patterns
                          └→ pendulum    a chaotic double pendulum (two runs with initial angles 1e−6 apart)

settings only hands the image size (size 480) and the random seed (seed 7) to the six Drafts; the Drafts are not connected to each other. Each Draft's description gives the steps of the computation and asserts that check the result is right (a glider in the Game of Life moving one cell diagonally in four generations, the double pendulum's energy error being small, and so on).

Press "Generate Cards" and the Agent splits the six Drafts among helpers, and a thrush of a different colour for each helper writes and checks its own Card at the same time (Splitting the work).

MNIST · comparing classifiers (Draft) (mnist-classifiers-draft)

A demo that has the Agent implement the same problem as MNIST · comparing classifiers. Unlike the dynamical systems gallery, the helpers' work merges into one comparison at the end.

start → load → prepare → share ─┬→ knn ──────┐
          (implemented)         ├→ logistic ─┤
                                ├→ svm ──────┤
                                ├→ forest ───┤
                                ├→ boosting ─┼→ compare
                                ├→ mlp ──────┤
                                ├→ cnn ──────┤
                                └────────────┘
CardStateWho writes it
load, prepareImplemented. Pins the real MNIST by its Nix hash and passes on a stratified 5000 training and 1000 test imagesThere from the start
knn, logistic, svm, forest, boosting, mlp, cnnDrafts. No wires between them, and separate environments (scikit-learn, xgboost, torch)Helpers, one each, at the same time
compareA Draft. Waits for the seven results and makes a ranking and a scatter plotThe Agent, after the helpers report
  • Why they can merge: each Draft's description writes out the type of the output result (mnist.Result). Helpers cannot see what the others write, so without this agreement compare could not read them with one type.
  • What is checked: each Draft's description has the steps of the computation and asserts. Besides the counts, the 0–9 range and a minimum accuracy, they check properties that each method's result must have (kNN agreeing with brute force in numpy, logistic regression's predictions agreeing with the weighted sums, the forest's predictions agreeing with the average of its trees, formulas for the networks' parameter counts and so on). compare checks that the digests agree and that the accuracies agree with values recomputed from the predictions.
  • Why the counts are small: a project can run only one run at a time, so the helpers' runs wait their turn (at most 900 seconds per wait). So it uses 5000 training and 1000 test images, smaller than the finished version (10000 and 2000).
  • The answers: neither this demo nor the finished mnist-classifiers appears in the Agent's reference_read list or can be read with it.
